memoryText: Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Proverbs 31:30 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
This verse is the last great statement of the book of Proverbs. It sums up the portrait of the excellent wife, and it says what matters most.

“Charm is deceitful.” Charm is the ability to win people with a pleasant manner. It can be real and it can be a cover. It can hide a hollow heart. We have all known people who were delightful and untrustworthy. Charm alone is not a foundation.

“And beauty is vain.” The word “vain” is the same as “vanity” in Ecclesiastes: a breath that passes. Beauty fades. In a culture that prizes appearance, this verse says that it cannot bear the weight we put on it. This is not a criticism of beauty as such, which the Bible celebrates. It is a warning against making it the measure of a life.

“But a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised.” This is the heart of it. The thing that lasts is a heart that fears the LORD. The book that began with “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” ends with the same note. Everything in the long poem of the excellent wife flows from this root. Her strength, her generosity, her wisdom, and her laughter at the days to come grow from it.

Although the verse speaks of a woman, the principle applies to every person. Whatever we are tempted to rely on, charm, looks, talent, or position, will fade. What endures is a life oriented toward God.

For the Christian, the fear of the LORD is fulfilled in a living faith in Christ, who calls us to a beauty that does not fade (1 Peter 3:3-4). Ask God to make this the thing you want to be known for.
weekInReview: This week you finished Proverbs and began Ecclesiastes. You read the Sayings of the Wise, with their call to rescue those being led to death and their promise that the righteous falls seven times and rises again. You read the collection copied by Hezekiah’s men, with the proverb that iron sharpens iron and the command to feed an enemy. You saw how confession brings mercy, how the fear of man is a snare, and how Agur prayed for neither poverty nor riches. You ended Proverbs with the excellent wife, the portrait of wisdom lived out. Then Ecclesiastes opened with its stark verdict: vanity of vanities. In Psalm 119 you read of the sweetness of God’s word and its power to give understanding. The week taught that wisdom is lived out in speech, friendship, justice, and generosity, and that nothing under the sun satisfies without God.
reflectionQuestions: Proverbs 28:13 says, “Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy.” What do you need to bring into the light this week?
Proverbs 31 ends with the fear of the LORD as the root of a praiseworthy life, and Christ is the one who lived it perfectly. How does his life give you both a model and a Savior?
The Preacher says that everything under the sun is vanity. What is one thing you have been expecting to satisfy you that cannot?
prayerPrompts: Ask God to make the fear of him your root.
Tell him where you have trusted charm, beauty, or achievement.
Thank Christ for satisfying what nothing else can.
